coredata.dc:description: A weak bonding strength and poor water resistance of soy protein-based adhesives have limited their application as a bio-based non-formaldehyde adhesive in the wood manufacturing industry. In this work, a soy protein-based adhesive was developed by incorporating tailor-made core–shell hybrids, which were synthesized by co-deposition of biomass Tannic acid (TA) as “hard cores” and silanized phenylphosphodichloride (BPOD(Si)) as “flexible shells”. For the soy protein-based adhesive system, the incorporated hybrids were designed as reinforcing elements and crosslinker to construct multiple crosslinked networks, which are beneficial to improve the bonding strength, water resistance and flame retardancy of the final adhesive. For example, the particleboards could be made by mixing with soy protein-based adhesives which show a rupture modulus of 15 MPa, an elasticity modulus of close to 2000 MPa and an internal bonding strength of 0.44 MPa, an increase of 110%, 110% and 145% respectively were registered when comparing with those of pristine soy protein-based adhesive. In addition, the soy protein-based adhesive was also designed to be potentially applied in furniture particleboard manufacturing area, and the flame retardancy could be achieved by a synergistic effect of denaturant borax and flame retardant in hybrids. Consequently, the soy protein-based adhesive showed a Limited oxygen index (LOI) value of 28.7% and the V-1 rating in UL-94 test. Therefore, this work provides a feasible method to produce non-formaldehyde and multifunctional soy protein-based adhesives.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: A weak bonding strength and poor water resistance of soy protein-based adhesives have limited their application as a bio-based non-formaldehyde adhesive in the wood manufacturing industry. In this work, a soy protein-based adhesive was developed by incorporating tailor-made core–shell hybrids, which were synthesized by co-deposition of biomass Tannic acid (TA) as “hard cores” and silanized phenylphosphodichloride (BPOD(Si)) as “flexible shells”. For the soy protein-based adhesive system, the incorporated hybrids were designed as reinforcing elements and crosslinker to construct multiple crosslinked networks, which are beneficial to improve the bonding strength, water resistance and flame retardancy of the final adhesive. For example, the particleboards could be made by mixing with soy protein-based adhesives which show a rupture modulus of 15 MPa, an elasticity modulus of close to 2000 MPa and an internal bonding strength of 0.44 MPa, an increase of 110%, 110% and 145% respectively were registered when comparing with those of pristine soy protein-based adhesive. In addition, the soy protein-based adhesive was also designed to be potentially applied in furniture particleboard manufacturing area, and the flame retardancy could be achieved by a synergistic effect of denaturant borax and flame retardant in hybrids. Consequently, the soy protein-based adhesive showed a Limited oxygen index (LOI) value of 28.7% and the V-1 rating in UL-94 test. Therefore, this work provides a feasible method to produce non-formaldehyde and multifunctional soy protein-based adhesives.

ce:section.ce:para: In the wood processing and manufacturing industry, wood-based panels (such as particleboard, plywood, and density fiberboard) are widely used in the manufacturing of furniture, building materials, and laminate flooring due to their good processibility and economic benefits [1,2]. Adhesives are the essential components during the manufacturing of wood-based panels, and are usually developed from non-renewable petroleum resources, which during service life can give rise to unwanted detrimental organic compounds (such as formaldehyde, phenol, and toluene) due to volatilization and hence pollute the environment and endanger human health [3,4]. Under the concept of environmental protection and sustainable development, it is necessary to develop an eco-friendly and biomass-derived adhesive for the wood processing industry [2,5,6].

Proteins (such as zein protein [7], wheat gluten protein [8] and soy protein [9]) were reported as potential materials to be processed into adhesives because of its extensive availability, low price and processability [4]. Some protein-based adhesives for the interior plywood manufacture have been industrialized in North America. For instance, the soy protein-bonded plywood branded as “PureBond” has been available on the market by the Home Depot company. However, the pristine soy protein-based adhesive shows an inferior bonding strength and poor water resistance due to the weak internal bonding strength and inherent hydrophilic nature, which limit its practical application in the wood processing industry [9,10]. In order to overcome these shortcomings mentioned above, denaturants were added to decompose the highly ordered spherical structure and unfold the molecular chains of soy protein, which could partially improve the properties of the adhesive [1,11]. However, this method failed to enhance the bonding strength and water resistance to match the practical requirements. Subsequently, some novel strategies such as protein structure design [12], biomimetic structure construction [4], organic–inorganic hybridization [13,14] and chemical crosslinking [10,15,16] are considered to develop high performance adhesives. Inspired by gecko structure and mussel chemistry, Liu et al. constructed multiple crosslinked networks among soy protein substrates, modified kenaf fibers and tannic acid, and then a biomass-derived adhesive with improved bonding strength, water resistance and thermal stability was obtained [4]. Zhao et al. established a stable protein adhesion system by introducing core–shell nanohybrid elastomers composed of cellulose nanocrystals (core) and elastic polyurethane (shell) [9]. Obviously, hybridizations with the core–shell compounds, which served both as crosslinker and reinforcing elements, was proved to be an effective way to improve the performance of soy protein-based adhesives.

Although hybridization modifications with biomass materials such as cellulose [17], starch [18] and lignin [19] can be used to enhance soy protein-based adhesives, the low reactivity limits their large-scale application to make adhesive. As a natural polyphenol, tannic acid contains numerous catechol and pyrogallol groups, which exhibit excellent physicochemical properties similar to mussel-inspired polydopamine systems, and thus acts as a potential multifunctional reaction platform [20]. Actually, tannin and its derivatives have been used in the synthesis of resins [21], hydrogels [22] and functional coatings [23] due to their multiple functional groups and high reactivity. Therefore, it should be feasible to strengthen the soy protein-based adhesive by hybridizing with tannin acid based on a reasonable design. In the preparation of wood-based panels, besides meeting the demands of high bonding strength and water resistance [24], some functional designs such as electromagnetic shielding [25] and flame retardancy properties [26] are also required. In particular, the flame retardancy is closely related to personal safety and property loss [27]. Therefore, flame-retardant treatment of the adhesives and wood-based panels have become an important preventive measure [26,28,29].

In this work, we aim to prepare the eco-friendly soy protein-based adhesives with improved bonding strength, water resistance and flame retardancy and apply to manufacture particleboards. First, phenylphosphodichloride (BPOD) was used to react with γ-aminopropyl triethoxysilane (KH550) to remove the harmful halogen and thus obtained the silanized phenylphosphodichloride (BPOD(Si)). Then, the tannic acid (TA), as the multifunctional reactive platform, was used to induce the hydrolysis/condensation of siloxane under the alkaline condition to form hybridization (named as TBD(Si)) with stable silication interface. A stable protein bonding/flame-retardant system could be constructed by incorporating the core–shell TBD(Si) hybrids, which acts as reinforcer, crosslinker and flame retardant to improve the performance of soy protein-based adhesives. This strategy provides a feasible guidance for the development and application of high-performance bio-based adhesives.

Soy protein isolate (content of protein ≥ 90%) was obtained from Linyi Biological Products Co. Ltd. (Shandong, China). Tannic acid (TA), Phenylphosphodichloride (BPOD), triethylamine (TEA), tris-(hydroxymethyl aminomethane) (Tris) and 1,2,3-propanetriol diglycidyl ether (PTGE) were purchased from Macklin Biochemical Co. Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Borax and γ-aminopropyl triethoxysilane (KH550) were supplied by Sinopharm Group Chemical Reagent Co. LTD. Poplar wood particle with 10% moisture content were provided by a local wood processing factory (Jiangsu, China). All materials were used as received.
The preparation route of the TBD(Si) hybrids was performed by a two-step polymerization, as presented in Scheme 1 . The typical synthesis example is described as follows.

2.2.1 Synthesis of BPOD(Si). KH550 (13.95 g) and TEA (6.38 g) were dissolved in diethyl ether (30 mL) at 0–5 ℃ in a three-neck flask. Next, BPOD (5.85 g) was added dropwise into the flask which was dissolved in 30 mL of diethyl ether. The reaction was maintained at 0–5 ℃ for 2 h, then continued at room temperature for 5 h. The generated triethylamine hydrochloride salts were filtrated off. Finally, the product BPOD(Si) was separated from the filter liquor by rotary evaporator. (Scheme 1a) BPOD(Si): light yellow oil, yield 90 wt%. The spectra of FTIR and 1H NMR were collected as Figures S1-S2 in Supporting Information.

2.2.2. Synthesis of the TBD(Si) hybrids. TA (1 g) was dissolved in deionized water (100 mL), and pH was adjusted to 8.5 by addition of Tris. The as-prepared BPOD(Si) (3 g) was hydrolyzed by ethanol/water solution (Vethanol: Vwater = 9:1) for 2 h and then added dropwise into the TA solution to form a mixture. After the addition of ethanol/water solution, the siloxane groups on the silane coupling agents were hydrolyzed to get the silanol groups, which could react with the hydroxyl groups of tannic acid. Next, the mixture was stirred at room temperature for 12 h. Finally, the remaining ethanol was removed by rotary evaporator to collect concentrated TBD(Si) suspension (Scheme 1b). It is known that tannic acid is water soluble, whereas the TBD(Si) hybrid compounds prepared by tannic acid and BPOD(Si) are hydrophobic and would precipitate in due time (Scheme 1c). Part of the suspension containing 2% TBD(Si) was freeze-dried for chemical analysis and the rest of the suspension was used for the further preparation of adhesives.

In a typical process, TBD(Si) hybrids, borax (0.6 g) and SPI (15 g) were dispersed in deionized water (85 g) and mechanically stirred for 30 min at 55 ℃. Then, crosslinker PTGE (20% wt% of total soy protein isolate weight) was added during constant mechanical stirring for 10 min at room temperature to obtain a homogeneous adhesive system. The resulting adhesive was denoted as SPI/D/C/TBD(Si). Meanwhile, different soy protein-based adhesive samples were prepared, and the proportions are presented in Table 1 , and the viscosity data are showed in Table S1 in Supporting Information.

Preparation of particleboard. The adhesive addition amount of the prepared particleboard is over 15% to improve the flame retardancy of the adhesive and the particleboard while maintaining the mechanical properties simultaneously. Typically, poplar wood particles (170 g) were mixed with 200 g of the soy protein-based adhesive by mechanical stirring for 10 min, then the mixture was placed in an aeration oven (60 ℃) to adjust the moisture content to be around 10 wt%. The coated wood particles were manually loaded into the stainless-steel mold, and then pressed at 180 ℃ for 13 min to produce 5 mm thick particleboard with a mean density of 1.0 g/cm3. The viscosity of the present soy protein-based adhesive is more suitable for blending technology rather than spraying which requires a lower viscosity to prepare particleboard, whereas it could be reduced further by such as alkaline hydrolysis. Since the soy protein has to be crosslinked into a 3D network in a subsequent curing step, the final performance of the resulted adhesives may not be influenced too much by the initial molecular weight.

Fourier infrared spectrometer (FT-IR). the FT-IR spectrometer (Nicolet 6700 Thermo Fisher Scientific USA) was used to analyze the chemical structure of BPOD(Si), TBD(Si) hybrids and soy protein-based adhesive samples in attenuated total reflection mode, within a range of 400–4000 cm−1 at a 4 cm−1 resolution, using 32 scans.

Thermogravimetry (TGA). The decomposition behavior of TBD(Si) hybrids and the thermal stabilities of the cured soy protein-based adhesives were detected by a TGA instrument (1100SF, Meteler-Toledo, Switzerland), scanning from 50 ℃ to 600 ℃ at 10 ℃/min in a nitrogen atmosphere.

X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). The surface chemical element components of TBD(Si) hybrids were confirmed by XPS (AXIS Supra, Kratos, British) equipped by a monochromatic Al Kα radiation at 1486.7 eV, which detected the characteristic binding energies relevant to each element of sample.

X-ray diffraction (XRD). To investigate the inherent interactions of the different soy protein-based adhesive systems, the adhesive samples were completely cured in a 120 ± 3 °C oven until a constant weight. X-ray diffraction patterns were recorded by XRD diffractometer (D8 ADVANCE, BRUKER. German) using a cobalt source and 0.2 theta scan ranging from 5° to 60° at 45 kV and 30 mA.
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The microstructures of the adhesive samples were investigated by SEM (S-4800, HITACHI, Japan). All the samples were sputtered with gold before observation.

Residual rate test. The sol–gel tests were performed to investigate the degree of crosslinking of the different soy protein-based adhesives. The prepared adhesives were cured in an oven at 120 ± 3 ℃ until the quality remains constant (m1). Next, the samples were immersed in water for 6 h at 60 ± 3 ℃ and dried at 105 ± 3 ℃ to obtain a stable mass (m2). The residual rate was calculated using Eq. (1):
(1) Residual rate value (%) = m2/m1 × 100%
Five parallel tests were conducted for each sample and the average was reported.

Moisture uptake test. The water resistance property of soy protein-based adhesives was tested by the water uptake test. The obtained adhesive was completely cured to constant weight (m3) in an oven at 120 °C, and then determined by gravimetric analysis at a temperature of 50 ℃ and a humidity of 80%. The weight of the sample was recorded every two hours until it reached a stable value (m4). The water uptake value was obtained according to Eq. (2):
(2) Moisture uptake value (%) = (m4-m3)/m3 × 100%
Five parallel tests were conducted for each sample and the average was reported.

Crack observation. The morphology of the cured protein-based adhesive films was observed to study the cohesive strength. The adhesive solution (20 g) was poured into the glass dish and then dried completely in the oven at 120 ± 3 ℃. Samples of these cured adhesives were recorded with digital photographs.

Mechanical performance test. Mechanical properties were determined following the China National Standard GB/T 17657–2013 using double column bench testing machine (Instron 5967, USA). Internal bonding strength (IB) was measured by pulling the specimen (50 mm × 50 mm) apart in the cross-section direction at a crosshead speed of 0.5 mm/min; Modulus of rupture (MOR) and modulus of elasticity (MOE) of the particleboards (50 mm × 150 mm) were obtained by performing the three-point flex test at a crosshead speed of 3 mm/min. The designed ideal dimensions of specimens were determined from a particleboard panel as showed in Fig. 1 . Five parallel tests were conducted for each formulation and the average was reported.

Water soaking properties of particleboards. Water absorption (WA) and Thickness swell (TS) were measured according to the China National Standard GB/T 17657–2013. The particleboard samples (TS: 50 mm × 50 mm, WA: 100 mm × 100 mm) were soaked in water for 24 ± 1 h at room temperature. The thickness and weight measured before and after soaking were used to calculate WA and TS. Five parallel tests were conducted for each formulation and the average was reported.
Micro-scale combustion calorimetry tests. The analysis of flame retardancy of soy protein-based adhesive was carried out by a micro-scale combustion calorimeter (System Technik AG, WFK-66).

LOI tests. The LOI tests were carried out with a JF-3 oxygen index tester (Jiangning Analysis Instrument Company, China) according to ASTM D2863. The different soy protein-based adhesive samples and corresponding particleboards with dimensions of 130 mm × 6.5 mm × 5.0 mm were studied.

UL-94 vertical burning tests. UL-94 vertical burning tests were carried out on a CZF-4 type vertical burning tester (Shangyuan Analysis Instrument Company, China) according to ASTM D6413. The different soy protein-based adhesive samples and corresponding particleboards with dimensions of 130 mm × 13.0 mm × 5.0 mm were studied.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Chemical structure analysis of TBD(Si) hybrids.
ce:section.ce:para: The chemical structure of TBD(Si) hybrids was characterized by the FTIR, XPS and TG measurements, as shown in Fig. 2 . Fig. 2a presents the FTIR spectra of TA, BPOD(Si) and TBD(Si). In the TA spectra, the broad absorption peak of -OH appears at 3100–3600 cm−1, and the stretching vibration peak of C = O appears at 1700 cm−1 [21]. For the BPOD(Si), the absorption peak at 3100–3300 cm−1 corresponds to the stretching vibration of secondary amine, the absorption peak at 2800–3000 cm−1 is ascribed to the stretching vibration of C–H, and the characteristic peak at 1260 cm−1 is attributed to P = O groups [30,31]. By further analyzing the FT-IR spectra of TBD(Si), the characteristic absorption peaks at 2800–3000 cm−1, 1700 cm−1 and 1260 cm−1 correspond to C–H stretching vibration, C = O stretching vibration and P = O groups, respectively, can be observed. The new emerging stretching vibration peak of Si-O-C is also observed at 1091 cm−1 [32]. These results confirm that the silanized BPOD(Si) was introduced to the multifunctional reaction platform provided by TA, and thus the TBD(Si) hybrids were synthesized successfully.

XPS analysis was used to determine the surface chemistry and elemental states of TBD(Si) hybrids, as shown in Fig. 2b-c. In the wide-scan spectra (Fig. 2b), the typical characteristic peaks at 150.1, 188.3, 282.0, 396.4 and 529.4 eV are associated with P 2p, P 2 s, C 1 s, N 1 s, O 1 s, respectively. In addition, the appearance of Si 2 s and Si 2p peaks verify that the effective deposition of the generated polysiloxanes on the surfaces of TA by the hydrolysis and condensation of silanized BPOD(Si), and thus obtained the TBD(Si) hybrids [33]. Fig. 2c further reveals the C 1 s score-level spectra, which can be divided into five peaks, i.e. C-Si at 284.0 eV, C–C/C = C at 284.6 eV, C-N at 285.7 eV, C-OH/C-P at 286.0 eV and C = O at 288.2 eV [9,34], respectively. The results indicate that phenolic hydroxyl groups of TA are partially consumed after the silanized reaction between TA and BPOD(Si).

The thermal stability of TBD(Si) hybrids was assessed via TG analysis, and the results are shown in Fig. 2d. For tannic acid, less than 5% mass loss is found below 200 ℃ under nitrogen because of the release of volatiles, and the major degradation occurs at around 350 ℃, and the char yield reaches 25.4% at 600 ℃ [35]. However, TBD(Si) hybrids display higher major decomposition temperature (400 ℃) and residual mass (53.9%), indicating that the BPOD(Si) was successfully incorporated with TA [33].

ce:section.ce:section-title: Structural characterization of soy protein-based adhesive enhanced by TBD(Si) hybrids.
ce:section.ce:para: The soy protein-based adhesives were prepared by uniformly mixing TBD(Si) hybrids and glycerol glycidyl ether (PTGE) with the soy protein matrix, and then cured at 180 ℃, the preparation process is illustrated in Scheme 2 . In the cured soy protein-based adhesive system, the densely crosslinked networks are formed by multiple physical and chemical interactions, which is beneficial to improve the bonding strength and water resistance of the adhesives.

The chemical structure and components of the soy protein-based adhesives were investigated by FT-IR, XRD, TGA and sol–gel tests, and the results are presented in Fig. 3 . Fig. 3a shows FT-IR spectra of the different soy protein-based adhesives. The major characteristic absorption bands of soy protein are observed at 3272, 2929, 1628, 1516 and 1234 cm−1, corresponding to O–H/N–H group stretching, –CH2 stretching, C = O stretching (amide I), N–H deformation (amide II), and C-N stretching vibration (amide III), respectively [33]. As expected, the typical absorption peaks of epoxy groups from PTGE cannot be observed in SPI/D/C and SPI/D/C/TBD(Si) adhesives, indicating that the epoxy groups were consumed by reacting with soy protein to form crosslinked networks [36]. Moreover, a new peak ascribing to Si-O-C moiety is observed at 1034 cm−1 in the spectrum of the SPI/D/C/TBD(Si) adhesive, suggesting that the silanized TBD(Si) hybrids were successfully immobilized into the soy protein matrix [33]. These results indicate that a three-dimensional crosslinked network was constructed among soy protein, PTGE and TBD(Si) hybrids by multiple chemical crosslinking in SPI/D/C/TBD(Si) adhesives. In addition, the hydrogen bonds might also be formed between -NH-, -OH, and C = O on soy protein and the -OH on TBD(Si) hybrids, which was conducive to construct physical crosslinking [37,38].

To investigate the inherent interactions of the different soy protein-based adhesive systems, the change in crystalline structure was studied via XRD spectra and the corresponding crystallinity is inserted into the Fig. 3b. Soy protein-based adhesives display two broad diffraction peaks at 2θ = 8.9° and 19°, which belong to the α-helix and β-sheet structures of soy protein molecules secondary conformation, respectively [13]. The crystallinity of the pristine SPI adhesive is 19.0%, and that rapidly decrease to 15.5% after the addition of denaturants, which can be explained by that the denaturants hydrolyze and reduce the molecular weight of soy protein molecules [39]. With the introduction of PTGE, the crystallinity of the SPI/D/C adhesive is further reduced to 6.9% because the crosslinking reaction disrupted the inerratic configuration of soy protein polymer chains, leading to the difficulty in forming an orderly structure during the curing process. For the SPI/D/C/TBD(Si) adhesive, the crystallinity is only 0.8%, indicating that a completely physical/chemical crosslinking reaction has occurred and the formation of more densely crosslinked networks.

The thermal stability and the temperature of the maximum degradation rate (Tmax) of soy protein-based adhesive are shown in Fig. 3c and Table 2 , respectively. In general, the thermal decomposition of soy protein-based adhesives is roughly divided into three stages: Stage I (100–210 ℃) corresponding to the volatilization of residual water and small molecules; Stage II (210–290 ℃) is ascribed to the decomposition of small molecular substances, the breakage of hydrogen bonds and unstable chemical bonds; Stage III (290–500 ℃) is attributed to the break-up of the soy protein skeleton structure, including the decomposition of peptide bonds, and the destruction of C-O, S-S and O-N bond [4,40]. For the curve of pristine SPI adhesive, Tmax2 is observed at 306 ℃ at stage III. After the addition of denaturant or crosslinker, the Tmax2 of soy protein-based adhesive is increased. It is worth noting that the Tmax2 of SPI/D/C/TBD(Si) adhesives increases up to 319 ℃, which is attributed to the high thermal stability of silanized TBD(Si) hybrids and the densely crosslinked networks formed by the reaction among soy protein, PTGE and TBD(Si), consistent with the FT-IR results.

The crosslinking degree of soy protein-based adhesive was further measured by sol–gel tests and moisture uptake test, and the results are displayed in Fig. 3d. In the histogram of gel content, the gel content of pristine SPI adhesive without using any crosslinker is 76%, indicating the physical crosslinking was formed by hydrogen bonds. While that of SPI/D adhesive is significantly reduced to 57% due to the breakage of soy protein chains by hydrolysis. With the incorporation of the crosslinker PTGE, the gel content of the SPI/D/C adhesive is increased to 86%, which is attributed to the reaction between the active groups of soy protein and the epoxy groups of the crosslinker, leading to the formation of crosslinked networks and thus preventing the erosion of adhesive by water. The gel content of the SPI/D/C/TBD(Si) adhesive is further enhanced to 91% after adding TBD(Si) hybrids. Moreover, the moisture uptake of SPI/D/C/TBD(Si)-15 adhesive is reduced to 18% compared with the pure SPI adhesive (23%). These results can be explained by the formation of the hydrophobic polysiloxane layer on the surface of TBD(Si) hybrids and the construction of densely crosslinked network structures.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Morphology characterization of soy protein-based adhesive enhanced by TBD(Si) hybrids.
ce:section.ce:para: The morphology of different cured soy protein-based adhesives is closely related to cohesion performance and their photographs are shown in Fig. 4 . The cured pristine SPI adhesive shows poriferous and irregular surface structures due to the hydrogen bonding interactions and entanglement of the soy protein polymer chains [18]. After adding denaturants, cracks are obviously observed in the cured SPI/D adhesive because of the weak cohesion strength. Unfortunately, the existence of cracks and poriferous structures will cause the soy protein-based adhesive disable to resist external stress and water erosion, showing unsatisfactory bonding strength and water resistance. With the introduction of crosslinker PTGE, the obtained SPI/D/C film is smooth, confirming improved cohesive strength and film-forming property. The cured SPI/D/C/TBD(Si) adhesive showed a great shrinkage. In addition, due to the oxidation of the residual phenolic hydroxyl on the TBD(Si) hybrids during curing, the color of the SPI/D/C/TBD(Si) adhesive has inevitably deepened [20].

SEM was used to further observe the microstructure of the cured soy protein-based adhesive, as presented in Fig. 5 . Cavities are observed in the pristine SPI due to evaporation of water upon curing (Fig. 5a). After the addition of denaturant, some cracks are observed in the SPI/D adhesive (Fig. 5b), which is attributed to the breakage of soy protein polymer chains and the weak cohesion strength [18]. Subsequently, the moisture can easily penetrate and erode the cured soy protein-based adhesive network through channels, resulting in poor bonding strength and water resistance [9]. The SPI/D/C adhesive looks dense from the fracture surface, suggesting that the reaction between PTGE and SPI occurred leading to crosslinked networks (Fig. 5c). Interestingly, the fracture surface of the SPI/D/C/TBD(Si) adhesive is rough, and the TBD(Si) hybrids are uniformly dispersed in the soy protein matrix (Fig. 5d). As a consequence, TBD(Si) hybrids can disperse the stress to improve the bonding strength, and simultaneously prevent water penetration effectively.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Bonding strength of soy protein-based adhesives enhanced by TBD(Si) hybrids.
ce:section.ce:para: Besides the denaturation and the heat release temperature of soy protein, the hot-pressing temperature and time have great influence on the performance of particleboard. In general, long hot-pressing time can promote the adhesives to penetrate into wood, which is beneficial to increase the interaction between soy protein and wood matrix and thus contributing a firm mechanical riveting effect for the improvement of bonding strength. A high hot-pressing temperature is helpful to evaporate the moisture in wood and adhesive to shorten curing time. Therefore, the hot-press processing conditions were determined as 180 ℃ and 13 min to produce particleboard with a mean density of 1.0 g/cm3 according to the study by Li [1].

In order to study the effect of soy protein-based adhesives enhanced by TBD(Si) hybrids on the performance of particleboards, the rupture modulus (MOR), elasticity modulus (MOE), internal bonding strength (IB), thickness swell (TS) and water absorption rate (WA) of particleboards were measured according to GB/T 17657–2013, as shown in Fig. 6 . The MOR of pristine SPI adhesive is 7 MPa, while that of SPI/D adhesive can be increased to 8 MPa after adding denaturant. This improvement can be explained by the fact that the viscosity of soy protein-based adhesive is reduced by hydrolysis of the alkaline denaturant (Borax), resulting in an easier penetrating into the wood to form mechanical riveting. Studies have shown that borax could react with hydroxyl groups on proteins [26] or o-diols on the surface of cellulose [41] to form covalent bonds. Therefore, the improvement can also be attributed to the formation of borate bonds in SPI/D adhesive system. With the incorporation of crosslinker PTGE, the crosslinked networks constructed by the reaction between soy protein and PTGE improved the bonding strength of the SPI/D/C adhesive in the wood substrate. The MOR of particleboard can be further enhanced by adding TBD(Si) hybrids. Typically, the MOR of particleboard prepared by SPI/D/C/TBD(Si)-10 adhesives reaches 15 MPa. Moreover, the MOE and IB of particleboard prepared by SPI/D/C/TBD(Si)-10 rise from 930 MPa and 0.18 MPa to 1950 MPa and 0.44 MPa, respectively, marking increments of 110% and 145% when compared to pristine SPI particleboard, which meets the requirement of interior application in dry environments (Table S2, P2: MOR > 13 MPa, MOE > 1800 MPa, IB > 0.4 MPa). Table S3 shows the comparison of properties of particleboards fabricated by different adhesive. In addition, the adhesion strength of plywood prepared by different soy protein-based adhesives is showed in Figure S3. It should be remarked that the properties of the soy protein-bonded particleboards could be further improved by tuning the hot-compressing conditions. Schematic illustration of adhesive mechanism of the soy protein-based adhesives enhanced by TBD(Si) hybrids in particleboard is shown in Scheme 3 , in which three perspectives are summarized: (I) The crosslinked network structures were constructed by ring-opening reaction between epoxy groups of crosslinker and active groups in soy protein ; (II) The residual phenolic hydroxyl groups on TBD(Si) hybrids reacted with -NH2 of soy protein by Schiff-base reaction and Michael addition, and the siloxane at the end of TBD(Si) hybrids reacted with hydroxyl groups in soy protein and the wood surface [31]; (III) Borax in denaturant could react with o-diol on wood particle to form borate bonds [26].

As wood adhesives, water resistance of the adhesive provides a necessary guarantee for the wood-based panels to maintain the dimensional stability and mechanical properties under humid and warm conditions. Thickness swell (TS) and Water absorption rate (WA) of particleboard samples were tested by soaking in water for 24 h at room temperature, and the results are shown in Fig. 6d. Compared with the particleboard prepared by pristine SPI adhesive, TS and WA of the SPI/D/C/TBD(Si)-15 particleboard are reduced from 14% and 119% to 10% and 108%, respectively, due to the presence of hydrophobic TBD(Si) hybrids and the formation of crosslinking networks among soy protein, PTGE and TBD(Si) hybrids, which prevented water immersion and thus improved the water resistance. The reduction of TS and WA is helpful to obtain particleboard with good dimensional stability and water resistance and thus can be applied in the preparation of wood furniture.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Flame retardancy of soy protein-based adhesive enhanced by TBD(Si) hybrids in particleboard.
ce:section.ce:para: In the preparation of particleboards, a large quantity of adhesives is usually needed. However, the inflammability of the adhesives is a big threat to human safety. Therefore, flame-retardant treatment of the adhesives to prepare the particleboard is highly necessary. In this work, borax and TBD(Si) hybrid with P = O groups were used to prepare soy protein-based adhesive, which may be beneficial for improving the flame-retardant performance.

Fig. 7 (a) and Table 3 show the HRR curves and micro-scale combustion data for SPI, SPI/D/C and SPI/D/C/TBD(Si) adhesives. The Heat release capacity (HRC), Peak heat release rate (PHRR) and Total heat release (THR) for the SPI adhesive are 88 J/g·k, 144.8 W/g, 13.8 kJ/g, respectively. The flame- retardant performance of soy protein was slightly improved by adding borax (SPI/D adhesive). In the meanwhile, the HRC, PHRR and THR value of SPI/D/C/TBD(Si) adhesive were decreased by 23.9%, 24.4% and 21.7%, respectively, in comparison with those of SPI adhesive. Moreover, the residual weight (Rw) increased from 26% (SPI adhesive) to 33% (SPI/D adhesive) and 32% (SPI/D/C adhesive) at 600 ℃, showing a higher char yield, as exhibited in Fig. 3(c) and Table 2. These results suggested that the incorporation of borax and TBD(Si) hybrids inhibited the combustion and improved the flame retardancy of the soy protein matrix.

In addition, the flame retardancy of the soy protein-based adhesives and the corresponding particleboards was measured by LOI tests and the UL-94 vertical burning tests. As exhibited in Fig. 7(b), the LOI of the pristine SPI adhesive is only 21.6%, while that of the SPI/D quickly increases to 26.3%. As expected, with the incorporation of TBD(Si) hybrids, the LOI of the SPI/D/C/TBD(Si)-15 further rises to 29.6%, indicating that an effective flame-retardant system was constituted by borax, TBD(Si) hybrids and soy protein matrix. Even though the wood materials are flammable, the LOI of the particleboard composed of SPI/D/C/TBD(Si)-15 still maintains 27.6%. The improvement in flame retardancy of SPI/D/C/TBD(Si) particleboard could be attributed to two factors: (I) borate formed a glassy coating on the surface of wood particle during the combustion process, promoting dehydration and carbon formation [26,41]; (II) the formation of PO· radicals during the thermal decomposition of TBD(Si) hybrids, conducing to annihilate radicals [30,42,43].

The digital photos of SPI, SPI/D/C and SPI/D/C/TBD(Si) adhesive of UL-94 tests are recorded in Fig. 8 . The SPI adhesive was burned fiercely, and the violent flame quickly spread to the entire spline after ignition for 10 s. When the fire source was removed away, the spline continued to burn violently until completely burned. For the SPI/D/C adhesive, small visible flames were observed after the first ignition and then extinguished within 1 s after taking away the fire source. Following the second ignition, the spline appeared like a flame tongue and the flame was persistent for>30 s. The TBD(Si) hybrids were introduced into soy protein to obtain SPI/D/C/TBD(Si) adhesive. As expected, some small visible flames could be observed after the first ignition and then quickly extinguished within 1 s. Whereafter, the second ignition was carried out, and the flame spread slowly upwards in the spline and extinguished within 18 s, which meets the V-1 rating in UL-94 test. These results were consistent with LOI tests. In addition, the UL-94 tests were implemented for the soy protein-bonded adhesives particleboards, which showed that the SPI/D/C/TBD(Si) adhesive can effectively delay the burning of particleboard (Figure S4). In summary, an N-P-B synergistic flame-retardant system was constructed in this work that has been proved to be an effective way to prepare flame-retardant adhesives.

In summary, this study reported an effective manufacture approach of non-formaldehyde soy protein-based adhesive with improved bonding strength, water resistance and flame retardancy by incorporating tailor-made TBD(Si) hybrids. The bio-based core–shell TBD(Si) hybrid was synthesized by adopting biomass TA as “hard cores” and silanized BPOD(Si) as “flexible shells” via a co-deposition approach. TBD(Si) hybrids were well-characterized and then mixed with soy protein to develop a high-performance adhesive. For the soy protein-based adhesive system, the incorporated TBD(Si) hybrids acted as a desired reinforcer and crosslinker to construct multiple crosslinked networks, which were beneficial to improve the bonding strength and water resistance of the cured adhesive. For example, the particleboards fabricated by the SPI/D/C/TBD(Si) adhesive showed a rupture modulus of 15 MPa, elasticity modulus of 1950 MPa, internal bonding strength of 0.44 MPa, marking the increments of 110%, 110% and 145% when comparing to the pristine SPI adhesive, respectively, which satisfies the requirements of furniture particleboard manufacturing. In addition, the soy protein-based adhesive showed a Limited oxygen index (LOI) value of 28.7% and the V-1 rating in UL-94 test due to the synergistic effect of denaturant borax and P = O groups in TBD(Si) hybrids. This work provided a facile and effective strategy to develop a multifunctional and soy protein-based adhesive.
